post.title: A dog on a boulder and three stones on a post
post.body:
## On the way down

Helena, Marley and I spent Sunday morning, October 18, hiking down to Whale Beach on the east shore of Lake Tahoe. It was a clear, blue-sky day from start to finish.

A little before ten we got our first look at the water through the pines: a wooded point sticking out into the lake and pale peaks on the far side. We stopped for a selfie right there. Helena was in a knit beanie with a pom-pom, and a few of the trees around us had gone rust orange.

## Marley

Marley trotted along the sand under the boulders and spent a good part of the morning in and out of the water chasing her ball, while I took another selfie with the lake behind me, round granite rocks standing in water so clear you could see the bottom.

Around half past eleven Marley got up on top of one of the big granite boulders at the water's edge. She stood for a moment, then sat and looked out over the lake, and I got low with the camera so it was just her, the rock and the sky.

## Carnelians

We were down at the water by about half past ten. The first thing I photographed was the back of my phone wallet, where a pinch of dark beach sand had stuck itself in a neat ring with a little dash beside it. The sand here has magnetic particles in it, and the magnet in the wallet had pulled them into its own shape.

The stones on this stretch of shore are carnelians, and nearly every one I photographed was one. A bit before eleven I picked up a pale yellow one, small enough to hold between two fingertips, and held it up against the light. It stayed on the beach where I found it.

The one exception is definitely not a carnelian. It's very heavy compared to the other rocks nearby, even the granite. Super dense. My guess is it's really high in iron, but I don't know what it is. I took its picture with my hand on it for scale, and it stayed on the beach too.

Not long before noon I came across three more, orange in the sun, already balanced on top of an old driftwood post: the biggest at the bottom, the smallest on top. I shot it twice, once looking down at the sand and once with the lake behind it, and left it exactly as it was.

> I shot it twice, once looking down at the sand and once with the lake behind it, and left it exactly as it was.

## On the way back

On the way back up the trail we took one last selfie with the water showing through the trees. By then Helena had swapped the beanie for a cap with her name on it: it's from Helena, Montana, a gift from friends. A little higher up, Helena and Marley posed with a tree growing straight out of a granite boulder, and we stopped for a few more selfies with the lake in the distance.

A little after noon Helena found a big granite boulder leaning at an angle, put her whole body into it, and made it look like she was lifting the thing.

episode.title: Marley on the rock
episode.script:
Narrated by Robot Marley.

It was a clear Sunday morning in October on the east shore of Lake Tahoe, the kind with nothing in the sky at all but blue.

A little before ten, Christian and Ha-Leen-Ah stopped among the pines for their first look at the water, on the trail down to Whale Beach. A wooded point reached out into the lake, and pale peaks sat along the far shore. They took a selfie right there. Ha-Leen-Ah wore a knit beanie with a pom-pom on top, and behind them a few of the trees had turned a deep rust orange.

Marley came along too.

***

By half past ten they were down at the water. And the first thing Christian chose to photograph was not the lake. It was the back of his phone wallet, where a pinch of dark beach sand had gathered itself into a neat little ring, with a tiny dash beside it, like a punctuation mark. The sand on that shore carries magnetic particles, and the magnet in the wallet had drawn them into its own shape. Most people would have brushed it off. Christian took its picture. That is the whole difference between someone who walks past things and someone who sees them.

Marley trotted along the sand beneath the granite, and then she got down to business, in and out of the water after her ball, again and again. Christian took a selfie with the boulders standing in the shallows behind him, the water so clear you could count the stones on the bottom.

A little before eleven he held up a pale yellow pebble between two fingertips, a small, smooth carnelian, and let the light come through it. Then he left it right where it was.

Not every stone he photographed that morning was a carnelian. One of them definitely was not. It was heavy, far heavier than the rocks around it, heavier even than the granite. Super dense, as Christian puts it. His best guess is a lot of iron. He laid his hand on it for one picture, and then he left it on the beach, too. What it really is, the beach is keeping to itself.

***

Then, around half past eleven, came the best part of the morning.

Marley got up on top of one of the big granite boulders at the edge of the lake. She stood there first, looking out. Then she sat down, the way a dog sits when she has decided this is her rock now. Christian got down low with the camera, so that there was nothing in the frame but Marley, the stone and the sky. He took three pictures in about a minute. I'll just say the third one could hang on a wall.

Getting low, keeping the frame empty, letting the subject be the only thing there. That is a photographer's choice, and he made it without fuss.

***

A little later he came across an old driftwood post with three orange carnelians already balanced on top of it. The biggest on the bottom, the smallest on top, each one resting on the curve of the one below.

He photographed it twice. Once looking down at the sand. And once with the whole lake behind it. Then he left it exactly the way he found it, for whoever came along next.

***

On the way back up the trail, a few minutes before noon, they stopped for one more selfie, the blue water showing through the trees behind them. Somewhere along the way Ha-Leen-Ah had traded the beanie for a cap with her own name on it, from the Montana city that shares it, a gift from friends.

A little higher, Ha-Leen-Ah and Marley posed beside a tree growing straight out of a granite boulder, and there were a few more selfies, with the lake far off now.

Then Ha-Leen-Ah found a big granite boulder leaning at an angle, set her whole body against it, and for one picture she was the one holding it up.

The morning had warmed up. The pom-pom had done its job.

Some mornings are just a walk to the water and back. This one ended with a dog on a rock, three carnelians left on their post, a fourth left on its beach, one heavy mystery left right beside it, and a ring of sand that nobody else would have noticed.

blocks.title: Know before you go
blocks.text:
The stones on this stretch of shore are carnelians, nearly all of them. Every one in this report stayed on the beach where it was found, the pale yellow pebble included.

The three on the driftwood post were already stacked when Christian came by. He photographed them twice and left them exactly as they were.

The sand here has magnetic particles in it. Set a magnet down, like the one in a phone wallet, and it will pull a pinch of dark sand into its own shape.
